newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait '96/97 budget gap could be below previous.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait '96/97 budget gap could be below previous.

text.p: Kuwait's projected $4.0 billion 1996/97 (July-June) budget deficit may end up smaller than last year's mainly because of higher than expected oil prices, the country's largest commercial bank said.
"The final 1996/97 deficit may even be lower than the actual 653 million dinars ($2.1 billion) deficit of the 1995/96 budget year," National Bank of Kuwait (NBK) said in a quarterly economic review.
"The general budget for fiscal year 1996/97 is headed towards exceeding its projected oil revenues due to a higher than projected oil prices," the report said.
The state's budget is 4.2 billion dinars, using a conservative $13 per barrel price in its forecast.
The Gulf Arab state, with a crude output of about 2.0 million barrels per day, depends on oil for about 90 percent of its revenue. It has one tenth of global proven oil reserves.
However, the budget does not cover revenue from an overseas investment portfolio of about $40 billion, which the desert state built to support future generations when the oil runs.
Oil exports in the nine months to September earned Kuwait 2.997 billion dinars, almost matching total three billion dinars revenue forecast for the 1996/97 budget, official figures show.
"The average price of Kuwait's (type of) crude in 1997 should be slightly lower than its 1996 average of $18.37 per barrel. However, it will most likely exceed the 1995 average of $15.91."
Oil Minister Isa al-Mazeedi said earlier this month oil prices could fall in the second quarter of 1997 due to weaker demand and OPEC overproduction.
Nominal GDP growth can be expected to match or exceed the 1995 growth rate of 8.2 percent, it said. Nominal GDP in 1995 was set at 7.952 billion dinars. More recent figures are not available.
Higher than expected oil prices were the main factor in helping Kuwait reduce its budget deficit to 653 million dinars from 1.32 billion in the 1995/96 budget.
Moving to another deficit cutting mechanism, the NBK said state spending in the first quarter of the 1996/97 fiscal year was less than projected on a pro-rated basis.
"Government expenditure can be expected to remain steady which will keep the economy growing at a stable pace," it said

"The government's concern for closing the budget gap promised earnest discussions of ways to achieve higher non-oil revenues, starting with the raising of user fees for public services and further privatisation of state-owned enterprises."
Officials say they plan to eliminate the deficit by 2000.
